Enervate

/EN-er-vayt/ - the stress falls on EN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Enervate means to weaken or drain of energy.

Three straight hours of fluorescent-lit budget meetings enervated the new hire more thoroughly than any workout ever had.

Worked Example

Caring for newborn twins had enervated both parents by March: they spoke in half sentences, salted their coffee, and once found the car keys in the freezer — not ill, just emptied.

Enervate is the great test-day trap: it looks like it should mean 'energize' and means the reverse — to drain strength away. The e- is the 'out' prefix, and nerv- is Latin nervus, 'sinew': to enervate is, literally, to cut the sinews out. What enervates you leaves you slack.

How Enervate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sap

sap: to drain strength little by little, the way a slow leak empties a tire

exhaust

exhaust: to use energy up through effort — enervating things weaken you without your accomplishing anything

drain

drain: the plain everyday word for emptying someone's energy

Antonyms

energize

energize: the trap twin — this unit's own word, and enervate's exact reverse

invigorate

invigorate: to pour strength and briskness in

How Strong Is It? — tire → enervate → prostrate

tire vs. enervate

tire vs. enervate: Tire is ordinary and honest — a long walk tires you; it stops well short of enervate's deep draining.

prostrate vs. enervate

prostrate vs. enervate: Prostrate goes further than enervate — an enervated intern drags through the afternoon; a prostrated one is flat on the cot in the break room.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out - a form of ex-

Root — nerv

Root — nerv: sinew, nerve - Latin nervus

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb ending

Put it together

Put it together: E- (out) + nervus (sinew) + -ate = to take the sinews out. This is the unit's flagship disguise: enervate is NOT en- + 'nervate,' and it does not mean 'give nerve to.' Romans used enervare for actually cutting an animal's tendons; the word has meant 'drain of strength' ever since. The n belongs to the root, and the little e- in front points out, not in.

Use the root in a new word: nerve

Use the root in a new word: nerve: It took real nerve to dive from the quarry ledge — nerve in the root's oldest sense: sinew, the strength you call on.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / test-day critical

Enervate earns its place when something drains vitality without violence: tedium, grief, thin air, long waiting. Exhaust follows honest exertion; sap works slowly; enervate simply empties. Above all, never use it to mean energize — its unit-mate and mirror image — and expect the SAT to tempt you with exactly that swap. Nearby sits emaciated, which is bodily wasting; enervation is spent energy, not lost flesh.
